blocks.h: Polypropylene or stainless steel for a PW loop
blocks.intro: Polypropylene suits an ambient PW loop, sanitized chemically. Water for Injection (WFI) or a stainless standard needs stainless. A hot loop needs PVDF or stainless [whether we quote PVDF]. Limits, sampling and release are unchanged.
rows: The loop carries Purified Water (PW) for non-sterile products, rinses and washing.
The loop carries Water for Injection (WFI), or feeds a pure steam generator.
The loop runs at ambient temperature. Natural PP is rated 0 to 80 °C, and its pressure rating falls as it heats.
The loop is held hot, or runs routine 80 °C at loop pressure. Polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) is the plastic option; [whether we quote PVDF].
Chemical sanitization, written as a procedure, with residual tested absent at every outlet before use.
Your procedure calls for routine hot water or steam sanitization.
It names outcomes: materials compatible with PW and the sanitizing agent, drainable, with no dead legs.
It names 316L stainless steel for product contact, and a deviation is not an option.
Your auditors accept a plastic loop backed by its maker's ratings and your sanitization records.
A client's quality agreement names stainless steel for water contact.
The cause is known and designed out: joints, supports for expansion, or heat beyond the rating.
No cause was found, and your engineers will not accept plastic again.

blocks.h: Chemical sanitization, proven at every outlet
blocks.intro: Sanitization lowers the microbial count; it does not sterilize. For a PP loop the method is chemical, written as a procedure and checked at every outlet. Your monitoring shows whether the schedule is right.

items.t: Isolate
items.d: Bypass or remove the parts the sanitant could harm, as the written procedure lists them.

items.t: Dose
items.d: Fill the tank and loop: [PP loop sanitization method], at [sanitant concentration].

items.t: Prove it arrived
items.d: Measure the sanitant at every outlet before the hold starts, so no branch is missed.

items.t: Hold
items.hold: the operator, at start and end
items.d: Hold for [contact time, hours], with the tank and loop out of use.

items.t: Flush
items.d: Flush the tank and loop with Purified Water, outlet by outlet.

items.t: Prove it gone
items.d: Residual tested before use, at every outlet. The signed record goes to your quality unit.

blocks.caption: Published industry case, 2006
blocks.h: A published case, read as precedent
blocks.intro: In July/August 2006, Pharmaceutical Engineering described a polypropylene Purified Water loop at a pilot plant. Two of its four authors worked for a water system maker. The article describes another maker's installation.

rows.m: Its sanitizing chemical, USP edition and design are the article's own.
Clinical supplies; water for the product, equipment and washing
Also chosen over PVDF, on cost
The authors judged a simple PW loop does not need it, so plastic was acceptable
Samples from every point of use, three days a week. Today, WHO TRS 1033 sets three phases over 12 months.

rows.v: Over a year of weekly release testing
rows.m: Each excursion was investigated and closed, with a cause or follow-up tests

items.q: How is each note written and reviewed?
items.a: A named engineer writes each note from a real question; a named reviewer checks it before publication. Each claim names standard, clause and edition. [named author and reviewer, by topic group]

items.q: Can we cite a note in our validation documents?
items.a: No: cite the standard, not the note. A note is our reading of the clause; your quality unit decides how it applies to your site.

items.q: What happens when a standard changes?
items.a: We review and update the note and its review date. If the answer changes, the note says what and when. Errors get a dated correction line.
